fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. The raiders who came into the camp with the Arabs had killed all the older sons, so the people of Jerusalem made Ahaziah king (2 Chronicles 22:1). He was the youngest son of Jehoram. I think he never pictured wearing that crown.

Yes, his mother. The text says she was his counselor in wickedness (2 Chronicles 22:3). Her name was Athaliah (2 Chronicles 22:2). Ahaziah walked in the ways of the house of Ahab with her voice in his ear.

Destruction is right. The text says the house of Ahab counseled him "…to his destruction…" after his father died (2 Chronicles 22:4). Bad advice can sound friendly right up until the bill comes. Ahaziah followed it anyway.

Mesha is a different name from a different story, friend, and he doesn't show up here. At Ramoth-gilead the text names Hazael king of Aram as the one they fought (2 Chronicles 22:5). So the Arameans were across the field. Good thinking on a king's name, though.

Sennacherib doesn't show up in this passage, baker. The text says they went to fight against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-gilead (2 Chronicles 22:5). That's who stood on the other side. You picked a king, and it was a king, just a different one.

Right on. The text says Ahaziah went down to Jezreel to visit Joram, because Joram had been wounded (2 Chronicles 22:6). Joram had returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Arameans gave him. Sounds like a good friend, but hang on to that thought.

A letter is a thoughtful idea, baker, but the text says something else. Ahaziah went down to Jezreel to visit Joram, because Joram had been wounded (2 Chronicles 22:6). No letter is mentioned. He went himself.

Jerusalem isn't where the text sends him, friend. It says Ahaziah went down to Jezreel to visit Joram, because Joram had been wounded (2 Chronicles 22:6). Joram had returned to Jezreel to recover. That's where Ahaziah headed.

Yes, from God. The text says "Ahaziah’s downfall came from God when he went to visit Joram." (2 Chronicles 22:7). It wasn't bad luck or bad timing. The same verse says that when he arrived, he went out with Joram to meet Jehu son of Nimshi.

Elijah doesn't appear in this passage, baker. The text says Ahaziah's downfall "…came from God when he went to visit Joram." (2 Chronicles 22:7). That's the answer the verse gives. Elijah sat this one out.

That's the job. The LORD had anointed Jehu "…to destroy the house of Ahab." (2 Chronicles 22:7). And Ahaziah had been walking in the ways of that very house (2 Chronicles 22:3). When he arrived, he went out with Joram to meet Jehu.

Peace would've made for a calmer day, friend. But the text says the LORD had anointed Jehu "…to destroy the house of Ahab." (2 Chronicles 22:7). That's not a peace mission. Ahaziah went out with Joram to meet him.

Wall building is a fine job, baker, but the text gives a different one. It says the LORD had anointed Jehu "…to destroy the house of Ahab." (2 Chronicles 22:7). Samaria does come up later, when Ahaziah is hiding there (2 Chronicles 22:9). Rebuilding its walls isn't mentioned.

True. Jehu looked for Ahaziah, and Jehu's soldiers captured him while he was hiding in Samaria (2 Chronicles 22:9). Then Ahaziah was brought to Jehu and put to death. It's a heavy moment in the story.

Not quite, baker. The text says "…no one was left from the house of Ahaziah with the strength to rule the kingdom." (2 Chronicles 22:9). That qualifier matters, because it's about having the strength to rule. So this one is false.

False is right. The text says "…no one was left from the house of Ahaziah with the strength to rule the kingdom." (2 Chronicles 22:9). The verse is about having the strength to rule. It's a sober ending, friend.
